Research

My research focuses on trustworthy machine learning for healthcare, particularly emergency care. I study how clinical risk predictions can inform actionable decisions using electronic health records, clinical guidelines, and real-world evidence.

Research interests

  • Clinical prediction and decision thresholds. Developing and validating sepsis risk models across hospitals, and learning interpretable thresholds that account for clinical behavior and operational capacity.
  • Causal inference and real-world evidence. Using target trial emulation to study antibiotic timing in emergency sepsis care, including how treatment effects differ across patient phenotypes.
  • Knowledge-guided clinical AI agents. Connecting clinical guidelines, shared patient state, and multi-agent reasoning to support decisions across the emergency-department sepsis pathway.

My contribution

I led a behavior- and capacity-aware framework that maps continuous risk scores to interpretable Low/Mid/High decision tiers, and evaluated its stability in MIMIC-IV-ED and Stanford MC-MED.

My contribution

As a co-first author, I contributed to a guideline-grounded and graph-guided system that maintains a shared patient state across recognition, treatment, safety, and disposition in emergency sepsis care.

My contribution

I contributed to development and multicenter external validation using more than 2.2 million emergency-department encounters across UMN, BIDMC/MIMIC-IV-ED, and Stanford MC-MED. My work included cohort harmonization and Python and R evaluation pipelines.
